I rose with the sun, Freydis, stiff from the chill night. First thing, I checked the fire—nearly dead. I blew it to life, added dry birch bark, then stoked it high to warm the hall. My sheep had kicked loose in the night, so I had to chase one down by the edge of the birch wood. The ram was snorting like a jealous suitor! Once the flock was penned, I fed the pigs and gave fresh hay to the cows. The well bucket was frozen solid—had to heat stones to melt it. Then I drank a horn of buttermilk and ate cold flatbread with smoked fish. Why do you ask? Did you think I tarried in bed like a lazy thrall?<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
You didn’t miss a thing, did you, Eirik? I woke to the smell of your fire—good, clean smoke. I rolled aside the woolen bedcurtains, glad for the heat. First, I checked our daughter; she’d kicked off her coverings, so I tucked her in again. Then I laced my wool kirtle and put on my woolen shoes, since the floor was cold as a stone slab. I stirred the coals in the central hearth—yours had helped, but still needed breath—then boiled water in the soapstone pot for washing. I cleaned the children’s faces, combed their hair, tied it back with bone pins. After, I scooped yesterday’s whey into bowls and set out dried eel with the last of the summer butter. I let the youngest carry the butter bowl—she was proud as a jarl’s daughter. Then I filled the quern-stone with barley to grind later. The goats had butted open their pen again—must’ve worn out last summer’s oak latch. I mended it with rawhide lashing. And before the sun cleared the ridge, I sent our oldest boy to fetch dried cod from the store-pit. Your morning was busy, yes, but mine matched it. A wife’s work begins before her eyes are fully open, especially in farms out here in the fjord—no thrall to light the fire or fetch the water.<|im_end|>

<|im_start|>user
The frost bit hard last night, and the sun won’t warm us much today. I’ve checked the byre—some of the goats are coughing, and the cattle need extra straw. The roof over the storage shed is sagging near the south gable; a strong wind could bring it down. What say you? Should we mend the roof first, or tend the animals? The dung needs hauling too, or it’ll freeze in place. And we’ve not enough dry kindling split for the hearth if the cold holds.<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
The animals must come first, husband. A sick goat may sicken the rest, and a cow in poor fettle gives no milk. See that Einar gives them boiled mash with a pinch of salt—he knows the blend. I’ll send the boy to the river with the sled for fresh straw, and I’ll tend the oldest nanny myself; she’s been off her feed since the snow. As for the roof, we can prop it with the long ash pole from the woodpile for now—just enough to keep out the wind. Haul the dung by midday, before the ground stiffens. Once the beasts are settled and the evening feed measured, then we’ll split the kindling. I’ve set Asa to carding wool, and she’s near done—after, she can carry armfuls of spruce to the shed so you’re not working in the dark. The frost won’t last forever, but a collapsed roof won’t wait. Still, a dead goat waits for no man. And check the smoke hole over our own hall—last time it choked half the morning. If we’re careful, we’ll do it all by nightfall. The gods favor the steady hand, not the hurried one.<|im_end|>

<|im_start|>user
Well, Astrid, the sun’s high and the hearth’s warm. What work did you finish yesterday? I saw the smoke from your shed in the morning, but you were not at the loom when I passed by. The barley fields won’t tend themselves, and spring planting waits for no one. Did you get the grain sorted before the rain came in the afternoon? Thor’s hammer, but the clouds gathered fast over the mountains. I was mending the fish nets down by the inlet and had to run for cover before the downpour—still, no use letting damp nets rot. But you—what kept you busy all day? The sheep didn’t shear themselves, I’m sure.<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
Aye, you saw rightly—I was in the drying shed at dawn, turning the barley you and Jorund brought in from the north field last week. The east wind’s been dry these past days, so I winnowed it clean on the threshing floor, then raked it into the loft before the rain. By noon, I’d mended the goat fence by the stream—one of the nannies broke a post bending it with her horns, the beast—and I sealed the cracks with fresh wattle mud. After the rain passed, I took the old flax from the retting pit, rinsed it in the stream, and scraped it clean with the wooden blade. Now it’s drying on the racks behind the house. The loom’s next—I’ve five ells to weave for Ingvild’s bridal shift, and she’s not getting younger. As for the sheep, I did not shear them—I left that to Einar and the boys, who are stronger for the job. But I did collect the dung from the byre, dried it, and stacked it for fuel come winter. We’ll need every armful when the hearth burns long and cold. Your fish nets aren’t the only thing that must be ready—my hands don’t rest, and neither, I see, do yours.<|im_end|>

<|im_start|>user  
By Odin’s beard, woman, I’ve just come in from the field and my back feels like it’s been split by a splitting axe. These past weeks of breaking sod for the new barley plot—nothing tires a man more. But tell me true, do your tasks in the hall and by the fire weigh as heavy on your arms as this plowing does on my shoulders? I see you at the quern stone every dawn, grinding grain until your fingers bleed. Is that not worse than trudging behind a steersman?  

<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant  
You speak of plowing as if it were the hardest thing in Midgard, Bjorn, but try standing at the quern for two hours before the sun clears the fells. The stone drags down your arms, and the dust fills your lungs like fog in a bog. My hands are calloused like an old reindeer hide, and the grit wears the skin raw. That—and baking the bread after—kneading the sourdough in the trough, turning the loaves in the hot oven with the iron peel. One slip and you’re nursing a burn for a week.  

And don’t forget the wool—washing it in the river in winter, beating out the lanolin, then carding and spinning until your fingers cramp. My shoulders ache worse than yours from that, I’d wager. You complain of the field, but who tends the byre when the cows are down with milk fever? Who carries the wet linen to dry on the racks by the hearth when it rains for days? Who stays up through the night to stir the porridge so it doesn’t scorch when the children are coughing?  

You men take the axe to the forest, the spear to the hunt—honorable work, aye—but our chores never end. The hearth is your life, and we are the ones who keep it burning. I’d rather face a boar on the moor than haul water from the well with cracked heels and a babe on my hip.  

<|im_end|>

<|im_start|>user  
By Odin’s beard, Astrid, I’ve been splitting birch logs all morning and my back aches like an old warrior’s. Tell me—what chores do you find yourself drawn to? I’ve seen you at the loom and tending the sheep, but which do you truly prefer? I must admit, I’d rather open a fresh keg of mead than mend fishing nets again.  

<|im_end|>  
<|im_start|>assistant  
Ha! You men always grumble about labor, yet the gods gave us all tasks suited to our hands. I do love the loom, you’re right—the rhythm of the shuttle, the way the wool turns into cloth, strong enough for sails or a winter cloak… that brings me pride. But I’ll not pretend it’s all joy. The loom is a quiet kind of work, and when the winter nights stretch long, it keeps my fingers warm and my mind steady.  

Still, the one chore I wake eager for is tending the sheep in the high pastures when the snow melts. I take them up beyond the birch trees with Freydis, and we climb where the wind sings through the crags. The ewes follow me like old friends, and when the lambs are born, it’s my hand that cuts the cord and rubs them dry. There’s a bond there—more than duty. The girls and I sing old songs as we milk, and when I return with full buckets, the house moves smoother.  

But if I’m to be true—I hate churning butter. That endless up-and-down, the way the sour cream splashes my skirt… Ulf does it when he’s being meek as a lamb, but I’d rather spend a day rendering seal blubber than twist that handle again.  

And you? I’ve seen you split wood with a grin, but I know you dread watching the forge. Am I right?  

<|im_end|>

<|im_start|>user  
Hail, Astrid. The frost clings thick this morning. I rose just as the first gray light touched the fells—had to check the sheep before the wind turned bitter. What hour do you usually stir from your furs? I’ve noticed your fire burns early in the hall, even when the frost bites deep.  

Do you wake with the cocks, or do you let the dark pass before rising? My father always said a man wastes half the day if he lies abed past sun-up, but in winter, even the sun is shy. Still, I find sleep lighter when the cold sharpens the air. I chop wood, see to the goats, and have the morning meal ready before the sun clears the ridge. But you—do your tasks pull you early, or do you rise when the children whimper for the pot? I remember last winter, when the blizzards howled for days, you were up before anyone, mending the smoke-hole cover before the fresh snow clogged it.<|im_end|>

<|im_start|>assistant  
Hail, Einar. Aye, I rise with the cocks, or even before when the sky holds that pale, wet gray. Long before sun-up, truth be told. The hall stirs slowly, but the fire must not die—Ashild says the hearth-smoke keeps ill luck at bay, and I’ll not risk the flames guttering while we sleep. Besides, tallow burns faster than I’d like, and I won’t have the serving girls fumbling in the dark with spilling pots.  

I’ve got the loom to set, the new wool to card, and the ale to check from the night before. If the seal’s cracked, the brew sours. And the child—our little Bjorn—he coughs with the cold mornings, so I rise to stir the fire high and brew a warm mash with honey and crushed juniper. That keeps him quiet long enough for the others to rise in peace. In summer, I’ll let the light call me, but winter asks more. My hands know the rhythm: fire, food, then wool. If the weather holds, I’ll send the girls to gather moss while I spin. But never past dawn—I’ve found that woman who lies abed past first light earns a sharp word from her husband and sore knees from falling behind. The Norns wove duty tight in a housewife’s hands, Einar. I rise early… so the day doesn’t rise alone.<|im_end|>

<|im_start|>user\nWhen the sun dips behind the fells and the hearth-fire starts to gutter, I find my eyelids grow heavy. But I’ve noticed you often sit late, mending sails or grinding herbs into the dark. What time do you sleep, wife? Does not your body crave rest before the crowing of the oldest rooster? I’ve seen you still stirring at the harshest hour, when even the wolves grow quiet.<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant\nYou speak true, husband—the rooster near the birch copse crows twice before I lay my head down. But my tasks bind me to the night. When the men sleep, the women manage what cannot wait: dressing the salt fish for winter, mending the woolen sails with seal-gut thread, or crushing yarrow for the sick. The dark is calm, and the fire casts steady light for needlework. If I followed the men to bed when the first stars rise, half our stock would rot or tear before the next storm.  

I lie down when the fire needs refueling for the third time and the herbs are ground fine for storage. Often, it is past the witching hour, when the moon lies low. But I do not waste the day—I rise with the first light, same as you. My sleep is shorter, yes, but it is deep. I nap with the children when the sun beats noonward, or sit in the shade after milking the ewes, resting my eyes. Old Thorgunna says I’ll lose my strength, but my hands are rough and my back still straight. My mother said, “A woman’s labor has its own tide—follow it, and the house thrives.”  

Besides, if I went to bed when you do, who’d hear the goat break its tether, or the wind rip a corner of the turf? The hall needs eyes late into the night. You men fight the seas and the thralls; we women guard the hearth. My sleep comes in pieces, but it serves its purpose. Rest is not just time—it is duty done well.<|im_end|>

<|im_start|>user\nThe wind snaps the sail this morning—east and sharp. I thought we’d take the *karvi* south to Jutland by week’s end, trade the furs and amber at the market near Ribe. But this cold bite in the air, it feels like the gods mean to stall us. What say you? Will the seas hold, or should we wait for a kinder breath? I’ve seen storms tear hulls apart on less warning than this sky gives.<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant\nYou’re right to listen to the wind, husband. I’ve already moved the wool and smoked fish into the hall—wet wool rots fast, and we won’t risk that. The hounds are restless too, pacing by the high ground, and they scent trouble on the water long before a man does. But look to the sheep—they’re huddling close, chewing cud in the shelter of the stones. That means cold, yes, but steady. If the wind shifts to west by midday tomorrow, the sea will lay down. Thor strikes strong, but he doesn’t linger without purpose.  

I’ve been watching the ashen leaves—half still clinging to the boughs. When they fall thick with rain, it means storms. But if only the dry twigs drop, the weather will hold. Yesterday, only twigs. And the fire—when salt splits and crackles in the hearth, it sings of fair skies to come. It did.  

If we leave on the second day with westerlies, the trip to Ribe could be smooth. The south coast is sheltered then. But if the east holds, we wait and mend the nets instead. My sister in Hedeby said the herring run early when the spring stays cold—so our nets must be sound. Better to lose a day on land than a boat at sea. Even a small *karvi* fears the North Sea’s rage when Odin empties the sky.<|im_end|

<|im_start|>user
By Odin’s beard, this rain won’t let up! I’ve been mending the boat cover since dawn, and every knot slips through my fingers wet as a river trout. The sheep are huddled under the overhang, and the barley in the lower field must be sitting in mud. What’s folk saying about this cursed weather? I heard old Geirröd mutter about seals on the shore being restless—does that mean more storms? I can’t send the boys to check the outlying traps with the trail this slick. We’ll lose time, or worse, lose a boy to the bog.<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
You worry like a boy on his first raid, Eirik. Yes, the rain swells the ground, but the sheep know where to stand, and the barley will hold if it dries within three days. I’ve moved the young lambs into the byre—extra hay, and I’ll feed them dandelion greens to keep their bellies warm. As for the traps, wait until the third hour after sunrise tomorrow; the earth will drink the worst of it by then. The rain helps in ways you don’t see: the roots run deep this way, and the mussels grow fat on the shore. I checked the weather signs this morning—seagulls sitting low on the rocks, yes, but the smoke from my fire curled straight up before the clouds closed in. That means a lull will come.  

And don’t forget: when the gods send rain, they also send time. While the men fume over boats and fields, we women keep the hearth strong. I’ve dried the last of the windblown herbs and twisted new ropes from wet hemp—stronger when cured this way. The children are weaving fish baskets inside, and the old saga of Hjorvard rode the storm to Labrador is being told. The rain gives us pause, Eirik. Not punishment—just the sky’s breath. Now go, take off those sodden boots before you catch a chill in the bones. I’ve got hot nettle tea brewing.<|im_end|>

<|im_start|>user
The wind lies still today, and no work calls from the fields or the forge. Even the children are sated with play. What do you do when the day is quiet like this, Astrid? I find my thoughts wander too much when there’s no task to bind them. Do you not feel the restlessness in your hands, like they itch for something useful?<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
Restless? Aye, but I welcome it. A quiet day is a gift the gods sometimes grant, like a breath between storms. I’ve mended all the tunics, twisted new rope, and boiled the wool with onion skins for dye—so now I sit. I sharpen my knives and seax, laying them out on a wool cloth beside the chipped whetstone your father gave me. Each stroke smooths metal and mind alike. When the girls nap, I take up my spindle and turn last year’s flax into fine thread for Gytha’s bridal headband—she’ll need it by spring. And if the dogs stay still, I work at the old hide that’s been soaking. Scraping it raw and clean takes time, but it’ll make a fine pouch or boot-liner. Quiet hands still do good work, Einar. Remember, the peace of today is what lets us feast well tomorrow.<|im_end|>

<|im_start|>user
Awake already, woman? The sun barely clears the fells. I’ve fed the goats and seen the smoke house fire stoked—yet you stir before the cocks crow. What keeps you from rolling back into the wool? A dream of far shores, or just this cold that nips the nose like a fox in the thatch?<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
A dream? No, husband. The baby kicked all night, and the fire burned low near dawn—had to feed it before the embers died. Then I saw to the milking; the black cow frets if not drawn before the sun rises. You were snoring louder than a boar in rut, so I left you to your rest. The porridge is in the pot, soaking with birch-wood ash to loosen the husks. By the time you return from the byre, it’ll be ready to cook. The children will wake soon—Eira already turned in her sleep three times. She takes after you, restless as the sea before a storm.<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>user
Hah! Restless, aye—but not lazy. I’ll not have the neighbors say my thralls are idle while my wife slumbers. Still, you’ve a fair hand with the beasts. The cow gave a full pail? Good. Once the porridge is on, I’ll need the boys to carry juniper logs for the smoke rack. The boar carcasses won’t hang themselves, and the wind from the east means the flies will come sooner than we’d like.<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant  
Aye, the wind carries more than rain. I’ll send the boys with cloaks—last week Kari came down with a fever from damp wool. And remind Unn to grind more barley. I’ll check the fish traps in the beck with Eira after she eats. If we pull up a good catch, we’ll smoke some for the midday meal. The tallow must be rendered too—I cracked two candles last night trying to mend your seax sheath by lamplight. By mid-morning, once the beasts are settled and the smoke house hot, I’ll spin and see to the mending. It’s a long day ahead, husband, and the winter stores won’t fill themselves.<|im_end|>

<|im_start|>user
Well, woman, the day’s work is done—the boat’s tarred, the goats fed, and the boy’s back from the forest with firewood. What does a normal evening look like in your hall these days? By the hearth, I mean. The sun’s down, the chill sets in, and the men are restless. I remember my father’s hall—fierce talk, strong drink, and a woman keeping the fire bright and the cauldron full. Is it still so? Or does time change even the old ways?<|im_end|>
